newsitem.title: USA: Stocks roar to records as interest rates slide.
newsitem.headline: Stocks roar to records as interest rates slide.

text.p: Stocks surged in a record-setting rally Wednesday as optimism over the economy and the balanced budget pact helped push long-term interest rates to their lowest levels in nearly 18 months.
The Dow Jones industrial average jumped 80.36 points to 8,254.89, the third consecutive record for the blue-chip average and its sixth new high in the last seven sessions.
Other major averages also set records, and rising issues swamped decliners on the New York Stock Exchange as the relatively narrow rally of recent sessions spread to the broader market.
The gains again came on the back of a strong advance in the bond market that pushed interest rates broadly lower.

"What justifies this market is lower interest rates, and there's a real perception that we're looking at a long bond that could be headed to 6 percent," said Richard Cripps, chief market strategist at Legg Mason Wood Walker.
"If you believe that, then its certainly possible to be bullish on stocks."

The long bond, the benchmark 30-year Treasury, rose 26/32, or $8.13 on a $1,000 bond, lowering its yield to 6.33 percent, the lowest since Feb. 16, 1996, from 6.39 percent Tuesday. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.

The euphoric atmosphere on Wall Street has come as investors have been treated to strong corporate earnings and falling interest rates even as the economy continues to grow, albeit with inflation all but absent.
Meanwhile, Americans continue to plough huge amounts of cash into mutual funds, most of them stock funds, creating demand for stocks and helping to fuel the rally.

According to the Investment Company Institute, which monitors fund activity, $19.91 billion flowed into mutual funds in June, and while that was down from $33.52 billion in May, it put total combined assets of the nation's mutual funds above $4 trillion for the first time.
Even as the market's dizzying ascent continued, analysts said further gains were quite possible as long as the favourable fundamentals remain in place.

"If you get good earnings, which we have, and rates coming down, which can boost price-to-earnings ratios, then you can get a real multiplier effect," said Melissa Brown, director of research at Prudential Securities. "I think that's what we're seeing."
Financial and economically sensitive cyclical stocks again dominated the activity but were joined by high-technology stocks, which fuelled much of the market's rally last spring.
Among active issues, Fannie Mae rose 2-5/8 to 46-1/8, Banc One Corp. gained 3-3/16 to 56-1/2, Citicorp added 4-11/16 to 135-1/4 and Chase Manhattan jumped 3-5/8 to 112-1/2.
Strongest among Dow components were International Business Machines Corp., up 3-1/8 to 106, Hewlett-Packard, up 1-5/8 to 67-13/16, and Aluminum Co. of America, which rose 1-7/8 to 87-15/16.
Elsewhere, Clorox Co. rose 3-5/16 to 137-15/16 after it said earnings rose 13 percent in the latest quarter and said it expected strong results in fiscal 1998.
In the broad market, advancing issues beat decliners 2,066 to 833 on active NYSE volume of 568 million shares.
The Standard & Poor's index of 500 stocks rose 10 points to 952.29 while the Nasdaq composite, laden with tech stocks, added 15.73 points to 1,588.05, both records.
The NYSE composite index rose 5.14 points to 493.57, a record. The average price per share added 48 cents.
The American Stock Exchange index added 5.12 points to 645.32, also a record.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues also known as the Wilshire 5,000 -- ended at a record 9,007.363, up 93.760, or 1.05 percent.
